question: Sicily's National Government Agency for Water Instability has been exempted from the applicable rules to temporarily place material excavated in its dredging works to restore the seabed at the port of Mazara del Vallo in marshland close to Tonnarella Lagoon (known as ‘Colmata (Gap) B’).

Tonnarella Lagoon lies on the coast in between two Natura 2000 sites (ITA010006 and ITA010005) of exceptional environmental value which are also home to species protected by the Habitats and Birds Directives as well as Article 142 of Legislative Decree 2004/44.

The sludge, which has been found to be toxic by all previous analyses carried out by the National Research Council, has oozed into the lagoon and is visibly hazardous, containing as it does foreign bodies, viscous liquids, oil, rope, plastic, tyres, used gas cylinders and vehicle parts. Does the Commission intend to: 1.
ask the agency to ascertain, as a matter of urgency, the toxicity and mercury content of the excavated material?
check whether the storage of such sludge within an area of natural beauty is in breach of EU waste legislation?
call on the Member State to enforce Directive 35/2004CEE, transposed by Legislative Decree 2006/152, Part VI (Environmental protection rules)?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.6.2024) Member States are required to ensure that waste is managed without danger to human health and the environment, including without risk to water, air, soil, plants or animals1. Waste management is subject to permitting and periodic inspections by national authorities2, and hazardous waste is strictly regulated3.

Storage beyond a certain period should comply with the landfilling rules laid down in the Landfill Directive4. In relation to Natura 2000 sites, under the Habitats Directive5, Member States are required to take the appropriate steps to avoid the deterioration of habitats and the disturbance of the species for which the sites have been designated.

Without prejudice to the Commission’s powers as guardian of the Treaties, Member States’ authorities are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, including verifying individual cases of potential breach of the relevant rules6.

They are best placed to examine the characteristics of the specific waste disposal operations, such as the storage of the sludge and the physical properties of the waste, including its hazardous nature.

The Environmental Liability Directive7 (ELD) requires operators to remediate occurrences of environmental damage caused by certain activities, including waste management, and to prevent such damage from occurring in case of imminent threat thereof. The implementation of the ELD lies primarily with the national authorities.

The ELD entitles specifically interested or (likely to be) affected parties to require the competent national authority to act by submitting to the authorities their observations with reasonable supporting evidence. Where the Directive’s criteria are met, the competent national authority has a duty to enforce the ELD.
1 Article 13 of the Waste Framework Directive (WFD) Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of

the Council of 19 November 2008 on waste and repealing certain Directives, OJ L 312, 22.11.2008, p. 3–30, as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/851 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May, OJ L 150, 14.6.2018, p. 109–140. 2 Articles 23-27 and 34 of the WFD. 3 Articles 17 of the WFD. 4 Council Directive 1999/31/EC of 26 April 1999 on the landfill of waste, OJ L 182 16.7.1999, p. 1.

10–20 and in the Communication of 13 October 2022: COM(2022) 518 final - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers. 7 Directive 2004/35/CE of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 April 2004 on environmental liability with regard to the prevention and remedying of environmental damage, OJ L 143, 30.4.2004, p. 56–75.
